summary: Earthquake safety for ages 5–7: children over-learn a simple, rehearsable response — DROP to hands and knees, take COVER under a sturdy table (or against an interior wall away from windows if no table), HOLD ON until shaking stops, then tell a trusted adult. The teaching objective is embodied muscle memory via a real physical drill; an on-screen timed rehearsal is a useful primer and companion but is a scaffold that teaches the sequence and reasoning, not a substitute for actually practising the moves. The 'why' is grounded in a key fact: most injuries come from falling and flying objects, not building collapse. Act immediately rather than freezing, and choose sturdy cover rather than any spot. Myths to confront calmly: do NOT run outside, and a doorway is not safest in modern buildings. Keep the tone matter-of-fact and reassuring — preparedness, not fear.
misconceptions: 'Run outside as fast as you can' — dangerous; windows and exterior walls are the most likely to hurt you; stay put and cover
'Stand in a doorway' — outdated advice; in modern buildings a doorway is no safer and you can't brace — under a table is safer
'The main danger is the building falling down' — most injuries are from falling/flying objects; most buildings don't collapse
'Just hide anywhere' — choose a sturdy cover and hold on; not all spots are equally safe
'The safest thing is to freeze and wait' — act immediately: drop, cover, hold on the moment shaking starts

activities.title: Classroom Drop-Cover-Hold-On drill (real practice)
steps: On a calm cue such as 'earthquake, drop!', physically DROP to hands and knees straight away rather than freezing
Crawl under a real, sturdy table or desk to take COVER, protecting head and neck
HOLD ON to a table leg and stay put until the teacher says the shaking has stopped
Practise staying under cover through a brief pause (shaking can start again) rather than crawling out early
When no table is available, practise moving against an interior wall away from windows and shelves and covering head/neck
After the all-clear, each child names a trusted adult they would tell, and says a short sentence they'd say
activities.insight: A fast, automatic safe response comes from having physically rehearsed the moves — act immediately, get low under sturdy cover, and protect the head and neck from falling and flying objects.

activities.title: On-screen rehearsal: the room starts to shake
steps: Watch a cosy room scene begin to shake, then act fast
Tap DROP so the character folds to hands and knees
Drag the character under a sturdy table to take COVER
HOLD ON as the room rattles, waiting until the shaking stops
Replay a few times to get faster at the sequence
After shaking stops, respond to the prompt 'tell a trusted adult'
activities.insight: The three steps happen in order and under time pressure; low-and-covered protects you because loose objects fall during shaking.

activities.title: Sequence and sort: safe vs not safe
steps: Put the three steps in order: Drop → Cover → Hold On
Sort action cards into 'safe' and 'not safe' (e.g. get under a sturdy table = safe; run outside / stand in a doorway = not safe)
Answer 'Why get under a table?' and choose the reason: to protect from falling objects
Explain in your own words why to move away from windows and shelves during shaking
activities.insight: Each safe or unsafe choice connects to a reason: get low under sturdy cover because falling and flying objects cause most injuries; don't run outside because moving during shaking can make you fall and the area near exterior walls and windows is the most dangerous place; and don't go to a doorway because in modern buildings it is no stronger than other places and does not protect you from falling or flying objects.

activities.title: Label the safe spots in the room
steps: Explore a room scene and tap spots flagged safe or danger
Reveal why each spot is safe (under the sturdy table) or dangerous (by the window, near tall shelves, exterior wall)
Tap through a Drop-Cover-Hold-On poster where each of the three steps animates
Point to where you would go first if the ground started shaking
activities.insight: Builds the mental map of safe vs dangerous places and the three-step routine before or alongside rehearsing it.

activities.title: Coached walk-through with a calm helper
steps: Respond to a friendly safety helper who asks 'What would you do first if the ground shook?'
Talk through each step aloud as the helper coaches: drop, cover, hold on
Say who your trusted adult is and what you would tell them afterwards
Ask the helper any worries, and hear the reassurance that most buildings do not collapse
activities.insight: Rehearses recalling and explaining the routine and names a trusted adult, keeping the tone calm and reassuring.

checkQuestion: Let's pretend the ground has just started shaking hard, right now. Show me exactly what you would do, from the moment you feel it until the shaking stops. (Set the room up with a sturdy table, a window, and some shelves.)
checkAnswer: The child immediately DROPS to hands and knees, takes COVER under the sturdy table (or against an interior wall away from windows and shelves), and HOLDS ON until the shaking stops — staying put rather than running outside or to a doorway — and afterwards says they'd tell a trusted adult.
